Part 1: Geospatial Data Wrangling with R
This part is about preparing spatial data before analysis. I need to import the data, check the CRS, convert coordinate tables into spatial points, and do simple geoprocessing.

Load Packages

library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
library(knitr)

tmap_mode("plot")



Data Used

data_files <- tibble(

An sf data frame is still a data frame. The special part is the geometry column. This makes it easy to use dplyr and spatial functions together.


Quick Plot with Base R

plot(st_geometry(mpsz))









plot(mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"])








The first plot only shows geometry. The second plot colours the polygons by planning area. This is good for a quick check.


Plot Multiple Layers Together

plot(st_geometry(mpsz), border = "grey70")
plot(st_geometry(preschool), add = TRUE, pch = 20, col = "red", cex = 0.35)








The pre-school points now sit on top of the planning subzones. This tells me the projection is working.


A Cleaner ggplot View

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "grey96", color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(data = cyclingpath, color = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, color = "#de2d26", size = 0.25, alpha = 0.45) +
  coord_sf() +
  labs(
    title = "Planning Subzones, Cycling Paths, and Pre-Schools",
    subtitle = "The layers align after CRS transformation",
    caption = "Data: data.gov.sg and LTA DataMall"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








This plot is just a visual check. I use it to see whether points, lines, and polygons are in the correct place.

Geoprocessing Use Case 1: Cycling Path Buffer

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath,
  dist = 5,
  nQuadSegs = 30
)


buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

The buffer shows the land around the cycling paths. The distance is 5 metres, same as the demo idea in the course notes.

  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(
  buffer_cycling,
  mpsz_selected
) %>%
  mutate(CLIPPED_AREA = st_area(geometry))


tibble(
  selected_subzone = mpsz_selected$SUBZONE_N,
  number_of_buffer_parts = nrow(buffer_cycling_selected),
  clipped_area_sqm = as.numeric(sum(buffer_cycling_selected$CLIPPED_AREA)),
  clipped_area_sqkm = as.numeric(sum(buffer_cycling_selected$CLIPPED_AREA)) / 1000000
) %>%

The st_intersects() result tells which pre-school points fall inside each polygon. lengths() turns that list into a count.


Derive Area and Density

mpsz <- mpsz %>%
  mutate(
    Area = st_area(geometry),
    `PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / as.numeric(Area) * 1000000
  )


summary(mpsz$`PreSch Density`)

  0.000   0.000   5.154   6.449  10.908  35.602 


Density is better than raw count for comparison. A small subzone and a large subzone can have the same count, but the meaning is not the same.


Histogram of Pre-School Density

hist(
  mpsz$`PreSch Density`,
  main = "Distribution of Pre-School Density",
  xlab = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
  col = "#9ecae1",
  border = "white"
)









mpsz %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `PreSch Density`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#3182bd", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Pre-School Density",
    x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The histogram shows that many subzones have low density. A few compact residential areas have much higher density.

ggplot(mpsz) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = `PreSch Density`), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey90") +

    title = "Pre-School Density by Planning Subzone",
    subtitle = "Number of pre-schools per square kilometre",
    fill = "Centres\nper sq km"

This map is not from tmap, but it helps me check the derived variable before using it in later analysis.

Part 2: Choropleth Mapping with R
This part is about turning data into thematic maps. I use dependency ratio as the mapping variable.

Import Mapping and Population Data

mpsz2019 <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/master_plan_2019_subzone_no_sea.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(3414)

clean_count <- function(x) {
  parse_number(na_if(as.character(x), "-"))
}

pop_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/respop_subzone_age_sex_2020.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("Total_"), clean_count))


tibble(
  layer = c("Master Plan 2019 subzones", "Census 2020 population table"),
  records = c(nrow(mpsz2019), nrow(pop_raw)),
  columns = c(ncol(mpsz2019), ncol(pop_raw))
) %>%
  kable()

The course website uses a population table and a subzone layer. I use the same idea here with the downloaded local files.


Prepare Dependency Ratio

pop2020 <- pop_raw %>%
  filter(Number != "Total", !str_detect(Number, " - Total$")) %>%
  transmute(
    SUBZONE_N = str_to_upper(Number),
    YOUNG = Total_0_4 + Total_5_9 + Total_10_14,
    ECONOMY_ACTIVE = Total_15_19 + Total_20_24 + Total_25_29 +
      Total_30_34 + Total_35_39 + Total_40_44 + Total_45_49 +
      Total_50_54 + Total_55_59 + Total_60_64,
    AGED = Total_65_69 + Total_70_74 + Total_75_79 +
      Total_80_84 + Total_85_89 + Total_90andOver,
    TOTAL = Total_Total,
    DEPENDENCY = round((YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY_ACTIVE, 4)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(ECONOMY_ACTIVE), ECONOMY_ACTIVE > 0)

Some subzones are unmatched. This is normal because not every planning subzone is a residential area.


Quick Choropleth with qtm

qtm(mpsz_pop2020, fill = "DEPENDENCY")








qtm() is useful for a fast map. I use it when I only need a quick first look.


Choropleth with tm_shape and tm_polygons

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")








This is the basic tmap structure. tm_shape() gives the spatial object. tm_polygons() draws the polygons.


Use tm_fill and tm_borders

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(
    col = "grey60",
    lwd = 0.1,
    lty = "dashed"
  )








tm_polygons() is a shortcut for fill plus borders. I like the shortcut, but separating them helps me control the border style.


Built-In Classification Methods

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 5

text:
Final Reflection
This hands-on exercise shows the full flow from raw data to maps. First, I prepare the spatial data and check the CRS. Then I create useful variables such as buffer area, pre-school density, and dependency ratio. Finally, I use different tmap options to show how map design can change the way a pattern is read.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Data and study area
How were reported road traffic accidents distributed across the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area in 2022?
The analysis examines event concentration, timing, and interaction between nearby events.

Accident records: Thailand Road Accident 2019 to 2022, restricted to 2022
Boundary: six ADM1 provinces from geoBoundaries
Study window: Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Samut Sakhon, and Nakhon Pathom
Projected CRS: EPSG:32647, with metre based distances


The raw point map provides a first check of the event locations. It shows more reports in the built up central and eastern part of the study window.

section: Time pattern across the year and day
text:
Time pattern across the year and day


















Q4 has the highest total. The largest hourly total is at 19:00, but the heatmap shows several busy periods rather than one isolated hour.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Quadrat counts and regional density

The grid shows the raw count contrast, while KDE shows the smoothed pattern. The quadrat Monte Carlo p value is 0.005, supporting a nonuniform intensity.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Quarterly spatial pattern

The broad central and eastern concentration persists in all four quarters. Counts rise from 731 in Q1 to 1,128 in Q4, and the surface becomes stronger in the second half of the year.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
KDE bandwidth sensitivity

The 3 km map shows smaller local peaks. The 10 km map smooths them into a broad regional pattern. The central and eastern concentration remains visible in all three maps, so the broad conclusion does not depend on one bandwidth.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Nearest neighbour evidence

The median nearest neighbour distance is about 34 m. Clark Evans R is about 0.26, the G curve is high, and the F curve is low relative to CSR. All three results support short distance clustering.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
K function and trend sensitivity

K is above the homogeneous CSR envelope. After allowing for the broad 5 km intensity trend, residual clustering is strongest below about 5 km. Coordinate jitter gives R values from 0.264 to 0.295, still far below 1.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Fatal and nonfatal spatial patterns

Both event types share a broad urban pattern. Yet the observed Cross K is below the random labelling envelope. With locations fixed, fatal events have fewer nearby nonfatal neighbours than expected from random labels.

title: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Main findings and planning use










analysis
result
implication




First order
Quadrats and KDE show a persistent central and eastern concentration
Review corridors and junctions in the broad concentration area


Time
Q4 has 1,128 records compared with 731 in Q1
Compare busy periods with traffic flow, holidays, weather, and road works


Interaction
Residual clustering is strongest below about 5 km
Prioritise local corridor checks instead of one large regional hotspot claim


Fatal labels
Fatal labels show spatial separation under random labelling
Study road class and speed conditions before explaining fatal outcomes


Data limit
No traffic exposure or road network denominator is available
Do not rank provinces as more dangerous from event counts alone





Use the results for screening, not direct risk ranking. The next step is to connect events to road segments and add traffic exposure.

9.5 Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation: Moran’s I

9.5.1 Moran’s I test
A positive Morans I suggests similar GDPPC values are near each other. The p value tests whether this pattern is stronger than expected under the null model.

The global statistics describe the overall pattern. The local Moran map and the Gi star map show where the strongest local patterns occur. I read the statistic together with its p value because a large statistic without significance is not enough evidence.
The results describe GDP per capita in one year. They do not show change over time or prove a causal relationship. Counties outside Hunan are also not included in the neighbourhood definition.

title: Take home Exercise 1: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
This report studies reported road traffic accidents in the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area during 2022. The study area is defined as Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Samut Sakhon, and Nakhon Pathom.
The analysis keeps 3,586 geocoded accident records inside the study window. Counts rise from 731 events in the first quarter to 1,128 in the fourth quarter. A quadrat test, the Clark Evans test, G and F functions, and a Monte Carlo K envelope all show strong departure from complete spatial randomness. A sensitivity check that adjusts for the broad 5 km intensity trend still finds residual clustering at short distances, while the broader pattern becomes much weaker.
Fatal and nonfatal events share the same broad urban concentration. However, a random labelling Cross K envelope gives a more careful result than the simple Poisson curve: fatal events have fewer nearby nonfatal neighbours than expected when the observed locations are fixed and the fatal labels are randomly reassigned. This contrast shows why the choice of reference model matters.
The results identify where reported accidents are concentrated, but they do not measure the probability of an accident. The dataset has no traffic volume, road length, population at risk, or exposure measure. Therefore, the findings should support screening and resource planning, not causal claims or direct risk ranking.

text:
Research question and objectives
The main question is:

How were reported road traffic accidents distributed across the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area in 2022, and what evidence is there of interaction between nearby accident events?

The analysis has five objectives:

Prepare a clean point layer from the accident table and a clear spatial study window.
Describe how accident intensity varies across the study area and across time.
Test whether nearby accident events are more common than expected under a complete spatial randomness reference.
Check whether short distance interaction remains after accounting for the broad spatial intensity trend and repeated coordinates.
Translate the evidence into practical road safety planning ideas while stating the limits of the data.

Data sources
The core accident data are from the Kaggle dataset specified in the course brief. The original file covers approximately 2019 to 2022. I use the 2022 records only, as required for this dataset option. The local CSV is a smaller copy containing the six provinces used for the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area. It keeps records with missing coordinates so that the quality checks remain visible.
The administrative boundary is the geoBoundaries Thailand ADM1 open dataset. The six province polygons are merged into one observation window. The boundary data are used to define the analysis area, not to claim that all accidents in a province have the same level of exposure.

Point event and time window
One row in the accident table is treated as one reported accident event. The acc_code field is used as the event identifier. Repeated coordinates are kept when the event identifiers are different. Several accidents can happen at the same reported location, so removing all duplicated coordinates would remove real event records.
The temporal window is 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2022. The month and hour variables are derived from incident_datetime. The main point pattern analysis is spatial. The monthly and hourly summaries provide a time based first order view without claiming a full space time model.

text:
First order analysis
First order analysis asks how event intensity varies across the study area. I use province summaries, monthly counts, hourly counts, and kernel density estimation. The counts describe the data directly. The KDE gives a smooth spatial view of local concentration.

Province level event summary

Kernel density estimation

accident_window <- as.owin(st_geometry(gma_boundary))

accident_ppp <- ppp(
  x = accident_coords[, "X"],
  y = accident_coords[, "Y"],
  window = accident_window,
  marks = accidents_sf$fatality_class
)

accident_ppp_unmarked <- unmark(accident_ppp)

point_pattern_summary <- tibble(
  points = npoints(accident_ppp_unmarked),
  window_area_sqkm = spatstat.geom::area.owin(Window(accident_ppp_unmarked)) / 1000000,
  mean_intensity_per_sqkm = intensity(accident_ppp_unmarked) * 1000000,
  duplicated_coordinates = sum(duplicated(accident_coords))
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

The point process keeps repeated locations because they represent separate accident IDs. spatstat reports the duplicated point warning for this reason. The warning is documented rather than hidden.


Quadrat count pattern
A quadrat map gives a direct unsmoothed view of how the event count varies across the window. I use a 6 by 6 grid and a Monte Carlo quadrat test with 199 simulations. The simulated test avoids relying only on the chi square approximation when some boundary cells are small.

set.seed(626)

quadrat_counts <- quadratcount(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  nx = 6,
  ny = 6
)

quadrat_mc <- quadrat.test(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  nx = 6,
  ny = 6,
  alternative = "clustered",
  method = "MonteCarlo",
  nsim = 199
)

quadrat_result <- tibble(
  grid = "6 by 6",
  chi_square = unname(quadrat_mc$statistic),
  simulated_p_value = quadrat_mc$p.value
) %>%
  mutate(
    chi_square = round(chi_square, 2),
    simulated_p_value = signif(simulated_p_value, 3)
  )

The cells covering central Bangkok and the eastern urban corridor contain many more records than most outer cells. The Monte Carlo p value is 0.005, which is the smallest value available from 199 simulations. This supports a nonuniform first order intensity and explains why homogeneous CSR is only a starting reference.

kde_5km <- density(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  sigma = 5000,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

plot(kde_5km, main = "Kernel density of reported accidents, 5 km bandwidth")
plot(accident_ppp_unmarked, add = TRUE, pch = 20, cex = 0.18, col = "black")








The KDE highlights local concentration rather than only showing raw points. A 5 km bandwidth gives a regional view. It smooths the data, so the map should not be read as an exact boundary of an accident hotspot.


Quarterly spatial change
The four quarters have equal three month durations, so their raw KDE surfaces can be compared on one common colour scale. This checks whether the main spatial concentration is stable through the year or driven by one period.

  mutate(quarter = factor(
    paste0("Q", quarter(incident_datetime)),
    levels = paste0("Q", 1:4)

  quarter_points <- accidents_sf$quarter == q
  ppp(
    x = accident_coords[quarter_points, "X"],

    window = accident_window

})

quarter_kdes <- map(
  quarter_patterns,
  ~ density(.x, sigma = 5000, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian")
)

quarter_zmax <- max(map_dbl(

The central and eastern concentration remains visible in every quarter, while the surface becomes stronger and more connected in the second half of the year. Animated quarterly point pattern
The static KDE panels are best for direct comparison. The animated plot below adds a second view: use Play or the slider to move through the four quarterly point patterns, and hover over a point to inspect the record.

title: Take home Exercise 1: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Second order analysis
Second order analysis asks how events relate to other events across distance. The reference model is complete spatial randomness, or CSR. Under CSR, events are placed independently and uniformly inside the study window. This is a simple benchmark. It is useful for detecting departure from random placement, but it is not a complete model of traffic or road design.

Nearest neighbour and Clark Evans test

nearest_distances <- nndist(accident_ppp_unmarked)

nearest_summary <- tibble(
  minimum_m = min(nearest_distances),
  median_m = median(nearest_distances),
  mean_m = mean(nearest_distances),
  ninetieth_percentile_m = quantile(nearest_distances, 0.9)
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

kable(nearest_summary)

    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(nearest_distances),
    color = "#d7301f",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Nearest neighbour distances, displayed to 1 km",
    subtitle = "The dashed line marks the median distance",
    x = "Distance in metres",
    y = "Number of events"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The median nearest neighbour distance is about 34 m, while the mean is about 192 m. The long right tail raises the mean, and the zero distances reflect repeated reported coordinates. The distribution therefore motivates both a nearest neighbour test and the separate coordinate jitter check below.

clark_evans_z <- clarkevans.test(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  correction = "none",
  alternative = "clustered"
)

clark_evans_mc <- clarkevans.test(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  correction = "none",
  alternative = "clustered",
  method = "MonteCarlo",
  nsim = 39
)

clark_evans_table <- tibble(
  test = c("Clark Evans z test", "Clark Evans Monte Carlo"),
  R_value = c(
    unname(clark_evans_z$statistic["R"]),
    unname(clark_evans_mc$statistic["R"])
  ),
  p_value = c(clark_evans_z$p.value, clark_evans_mc$p.value)
) %>%
  mutate(R_value = round(R_value, 4))

The (R) value is well below 1 and the test supports the clustered alternative. In practical terms, the observed nearest neighbour distances are much shorter than expected under CSR. The Monte Carlo result uses 39 simulated CSR patterns with the same number of points. It is a small simulation for a transparent and quick report, so it should be read as supporting evidence rather than a final probability statement.


Repeated coordinate sensitivity
There are 321 coordinate rows that repeat an earlier longitude and latitude pair. The records have different accident IDs, so they remain in the main analysis. However, repeated geocoding locations can make the nearest neighbour result look more clustered at very short distances. I therefore repeat the Clark Evans calculation after randomly moving every point by at most 25 m and 100 m. These distances are very small compared with the 5 km KDE and 15 km K function ranges.

G and F functions
The G function describes the distance from each event to its nearest other event. The F function describes the distance from random locations in the window to the nearest event. I use the Kaplan Meier style correction available in spatstat and compare the observed curves with CSR envelopes.

g_csr <- envelope(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  Gest,
  nsim = 39,
  nrank = 1,
  correction = "rs",
  rmax = 5000,
  nr = 64,
  verbose = FALSE
)

  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  Fest,
  nsim = 39,
  nrank = 1,
  correction = "rs",
  rmax = 5000,
  nr = 64,
  verbose = FALSE
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

At short distances, the observed G curve is above the CSR envelope. This means that very close event pairs occur more often than the CSR reference suggests. The observed F curve is below the CSR envelope, which is also consistent with clustering because random locations are more likely to fall in large empty parts of the window. At larger distances, edge effects and the shape of the study window become more important.


K function with a Monte Carlo envelope
The K function counts neighbours within increasing distance bands. I use Ripley isotropic correction and a 39 simulation CSR envelope. The distance range is limited to 15 km to keep the interpretation focused on local and regional interaction.

set.seed(626)

k_csr <- envelope(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  Kest,
  nsim = 39,
  nrank = 1,
  correction = "Ripley",
  rmax = 15000,
  nr = 64,
  verbose = FALSE
)


plot(k_csr, main = "K function with Monte Carlo CSR envelope")








The observed K curve is above the simulation envelope across the selected range. This supports clustering beyond the variation expected from a homogeneous CSR process. K uses all neighbours within a distance, so it gives a broader view than the nearest neighbour result.


Inhomogeneous K sensitivity
The homogeneous CSR comparison assumes a constant event intensity across the study window. The KDE maps show that this is unrealistic here. I therefore estimate a 5 km spatial intensity surface and use leave one out values at the accident points in an inhomogeneous K function. This is a sensitivity check for the large scale trend, not an exposure adjusted risk model.

  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  sigma = 5000,
  edge = TRUE,
  at = "points",
  leaveoneout = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

k_inhom <- Kinhom(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  lambda = lambda_5km_points,
  correction = "translate",
  rmax = 15000,
  nr = 64
)

l_inhom <- Linhom(
  accident_ppp_unmarked,
  lambda = lambda_5km_points,
  correction = "translate",
  rmax = 15000,

title: Take home Exercise 1: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Public safety planning and management
The results can support an initial screening workflow for road safety planning. First, the province summary and KDE can help agencies decide where to review road segments, junctions, and response coverage. Bangkok and the nearby provinces have many reported records, but the counts should be checked against traffic volume and road length before funds are allocated.
Second, the monthly and hourly patterns can help with staffing and patrol planning. The figures show when reports are more common in this dataset. A transport agency could compare these time periods with traffic flow, weather, holidays, and road works before changing schedules.
Third, the inhomogeneous K result narrows the field review scale. The strongest residual interaction occurs within about 5 km after the broad intensity trend is considered. Nearby events may reflect repeated issues on the same corridors, junction design, speed conditions, or reporting concentration. A practical next step would be to connect the points to a road network and inspect the highest concentration segments in the field.
The analysis does not support a direct claim that a province is more dangerous. The data do not include exposure, traffic volume, road length, population, enforcement, or the number of trips. The boundary also combines dense urban districts with less dense outer areas. The recommendations should therefore be used to prioritise further investigation and not as a final risk ranking.

title: Take home Exercise 1: Road Traffic Accident Patterns in Bangkok
text:
Conclusion
After filtering the supplied 2019 to 2022 table to 2022 and the six selected provinces, 3,586 valid accident points remained inside the study window. First order results show clear differences across provinces, months, hours, quarters, quadrats, and local density. Homogeneous CSR tests give consistent evidence of clustering. The duplicate coordinate sensitivity check keeps the Clark Evans R value well below 1 after 25 m and 100 m jitter. After allowing for the broad 5 km intensity trend, the strongest residual clustering remains within roughly 5 km.
The marked analysis gives a useful qualification. Fatal and nonfatal events share the broad urban concentration and the simple Poisson Cross K curve is high. Once all accident locations are fixed and only the labels are randomised, the observed Cross K curve falls below the envelope. The data therefore support broad co location but not attraction between fatal and nonfatal labels.
The safest conclusion is that reported accidents form concentrated spatial patterns that deserve closer road level investigation. The results are useful for identifying where to ask the next question. They are not enough to estimate causal effects or rank danger without traffic exposure and road network information.

12.9 Spatially Constrained Clustering: ClustGeo Method

12.9.1 A short note about ClustGeo package
ClustGeo combines attribute differences with geographical distances. Alpha controls their balance. A distance penalty encourages geographical proximity, but does not guarantee connected regions in the way SKATER does.


12.9.2 Ward-like hierarchical clustering: ClustGeo
This first ClustGeo example uses only the ICT distance matrix. It is the baseline for the next spatial comparison.

nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, 
            k = 6, 
            border = 2:5)









12.9.2.1 Mapping the clusters formed

groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k=6))


shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)


qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")











12.9.3 Spatially Constrained Hierarchical Clustering
The geographical matrix uses distances between polygon geometries, as in the chapter. Touching polygons have zero distance. I inspect the alpha curves and retain 0.2 for comparison with the course example.

dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)


cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K=6, graph = TRUE)
















clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)


groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k=6))


shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)


qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER")

My Comparison and Conclusion
The non geographical ClustGeo profiles show that Cluster 4 has about 744 TV owning households and 651 mobile phone owning households per 1,000 households. Cluster 5 has about 224 and 132 respectively. This is a large difference in these two types of ICT access. Radio tells a different story: its highest group mean is in Cluster 3, so the groups cannot simply be ranked from best to worst across every indicator.
The three methods answer slightly different questions. Ordinary hierarchical clustering groups similar ICT profiles regardless of location. SKATER creates regions connected through neighbouring townships. ClustGeo lets me trade some attribute similarity for geographical proximity.
I put the final three maps together below. The labels are local to each method, so I compare the shapes and fragmentation rather than assuming that the colours identify the same groups.

tmap_arrange(
  qtm(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER") + tm_title("Hierarchical clustering"),
  qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER") + tm_title("SKATER"),
  qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER") + tm_title("ClustGeo: alpha = 0.2"),
  ncol = 3)

  SKATER = as.integer(table(factor(shan_sf_spatialcluster$SP_CLUSTER, levels = 1:6))),
  ClustGeo = as.integer(table(factor(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER, levels = 1:6)))

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 17. I measure how easy it is to reach eldercare centres from different parts of Singapore. Singapore is divided into small hexagons, and each hexagon gets an accessibility score.
I use three methods from the chapter: Hansen’s potential model, KD2SFCA and the Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM). They all use the road network distance between each hexagon and each eldercare centre. They differ in how they treat distance and competition between users.

17.7 Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using KD2SFCA Method

17.7.1 Computing KD2SFCA’s accessibility
KD2SFCA is a two step floating catchment method. First, each centre’s capacity is shared among the hexagons within its catchment. Then each hexagon adds up the shares of the centres it can reach. d0 = 5 sets a 5 km catchment, and a kernel makes closer pairs count more. Unlike Hansen, it includes competition between hexagons.

acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            d0 = 5,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "KD2SFCA"))

acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)

title: Take home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Research question and objectives
The main question is:

Where did political violence concentrate in Myanmar between January 2021 and September 2025, and how did these concentrations emerge, persist, or fade over time at township level?

The analysis has five objectives:

Prepare a clean township by quarter table of armed conflict events from the ACLED records and the MIMU township boundaries.
Describe the geographic distribution and the time pattern of the main conflict variables.
Identify significant clusters, spatial outliers, hot spots and cold spots with local measures of spatial association.
Classify how hot and cold spots changed through time with emerging hot spot analysis.
Check whether the main hot spot pattern depends on the township boundaries by repeating the space-time analysis on equal area hexagons.

Unit of analysis and time window
The main spatial unit is the township. It is the level named in the objective, and it matches the Pcodes used by humanitarian agencies. The time window is 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025. The conflict variables are the counts of the three ACLED political violence event types: Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, and Violence against civilians. Their sum is the main variable. Reported fatalities are used as a second measure of intensity.

Only 94 political violence events (0.2%) have precision code 3, so removing them has very little effect on the totals. 53,910 events remain.


Point layer and township join
The coordinates are converted to points in WGS 84 and then projected to EPSG:32647. I assign each event to a township with a point-in-polygon join instead of the ACLED admin3 name. Township names have different spellings in the two sources, while the polygon join uses the official MIMU boundaries and Pcodes directly.
A point that falls exactly on a shared border can match two townships. I keep the first match so every event is counted once. A few events fall just outside the coastline. If an event is within 5 km of a township, it is assigned to the nearest township. Events further away, for example at sea, are removed.

  distinct(event_id_cnty, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(join_method = if_else(is.na(TS_PCODE), "Not matched", "Inside a township"))

    mmr_ts[nearest_idx, ],
    by_element = TRUE

  snap_rows <- unmatched_rows[nearest_m <= 5000]
  snap_idx <- nearest_idx[nearest_m <= 5000]
  conflict_ts$TS_PCODE[snap_rows] <- mmr_ts$TS_PCODE[snap_idx]

Reported political violence rose quickly after the coup on 1 February 2021. The total grew from 401 events in 2021 Q1 to 3,004 in 2021 Q4. It then stayed close to 3,000 events a quarter and reached its highest level, 4,026 events, in 2023 Q4. The 2025 quarters are a little lower, at about 2,800 to 3,000 events, but still far above early 2021.
The mix of violence changed. From 2023 Q4, explosions and remote violence were higher than battles in every quarter. The sub-event table shows why. Air and drone strikes rose from 88 events in 2021 to 2,977 in 2024, and reached 2,501 in only the first three quarters of 2025. Shelling also increased until 2024. In contrast, remote explosives and IEDs fell from 2,525 events in 2022 to 400 in 2025. Violence against civilians peaked in 2021 Q4 at about 780 events and then fell gradually to about 400 to 500 a quarter by 2024, although abductions kept rising.
Together, these changes suggest a shift from bombings and attacks in towns in 2021 to air power and artillery in a wider armed conflict. The counts show reported events, not all events.

Magway and Mandalay stayed high from late 2021, with about 170 to 450 events a quarter.
Other areas flared at specific times. Yangon had more than 240 events a quarter from 2021 Q2 to 2022 Q1, when urban resistance was strong, but fewer than 100 from 2023. Before mapping local patterns, I test whether each variable is spatially clustered overall. The permutation test shuffles the values across townships 999 times while the neighbour structure stays fixed.

Local measures of spatial association

Local Moran’s I: clusters and outliers
Local Moran’s I compares each township with the average of its neighbours. High-High and Low-Low are clusters of similar values. High-Low and Low-High are spatial outliers. The counts are very skewed, so I use the permutation p value (p_ii_sim, 499 simulations) instead of the normal approximation. Only results with p < 0.05 are coloured.

      value = mmr_conflict[[v]],

      p_ii_sim = res$p_ii_sim,

}))

Together they form one large block in the central dry zone around Monywa, Myaing, Shwebo and Pakokku. A second, smaller High-High chain runs along the Thai border in Kayin and Tanintharyi, including Myawaddy, Kyainseikgyi, Yebyu, Dawei and Thayetchaung.
There are 48 Low-Low townships. Most are in the Ayeyarwady delta (13), eastern Shan (10) and Yangon (9). Fatalities give the only High-Low outlier, Lashio in northern Shan, with 504 reported deaths while its neighbours had far fewer.
The pattern is similar for all five variables, which shows that the central dry zone cluster is robust. Explosions and remote violence add a High-High band through eastern Bago and Kayin.


Getis-Ord Gi*: hot spots and cold spots
Gi* looks at the total of a township and its neighbours together. A significant positive value is a hot spot, an area where high values are concentrated. A significant negative value is a cold spot. I use 499 permutations, so p < 0.01 and p < 0.05 can be separated.

set.seed(1234)
gi_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lmsa_vars), function(v) {
  res <- local_gstar_perm(mmr_conflict[[v]], nb_self, wt_self, nsim = 499)
  mmr_conflict %>%
    select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) %>%
    mutate(
      variable = lmsa_vars[[v]],
      value = mmr_conflict[[v]],
      gi_star = res$gi_star,
      p_sim = res$p_sim
    )
}))

gi_levels <- c(
  "Cold spot, p < 0.01", "Cold spot, p < 0.05", "Not significant",
  "Hot spot, p < 0.05", "Hot spot, p < 0.01"
)

gi_long <- gi_long %>%
  mutate(
    variable = factor(variable, levels = lmsa_vars),
    gi_class = case_when(
      gi_star > 0 & p_sim < 0.01 ~ "Hot spot, p < 0.01",

Of the 330 townships, 95 are in a hot spot class, 163 in a cold spot class and 72 show no pattern. The hot spot classes hold 59.5% of all events. The descriptions below follow the order of the legend.

Persistent hot spot
Only Pale in Sagaing is a persistent hot spot. It was a significant hot spot in at least 90% of the quarters, and its Gi* has no significant trend. Pale recorded 537 events. Its count rose from zero in 2021 Q1 to 56 in 2021 Q4 and stayed between about 30 and 46 events a quarter until 2023, before dropping in 2024. The neighbourhood stayed significantly hot even when Pale’s own count fell, which is why the classification does not change. Pale is the clearest example of long-running conflict in the south-west of Sagaing.


Consecutive hot spots
Seven townships became significant hot spots only in the latest quarters and stayed hot without a break: Nawnghkio, Kyaukkyi, Kyaukme, Kyainseikgyi, Yebyu, Mogoke and Shwegyin. They hold 6.1% of all events. Their average count rose from 9 events a quarter in 2021 to 43 in 2025, and it reached 55 in 2025 Q3, the highest of any class at the end of the study period. Nawnghkio, Kyaukme and Mogoke lie between Mandalay and northern Shan, where fighting grew after late 2023. Kyaukkyi and Shwegyin are in eastern Bago, Kyainseikgyi is in Kayin and Yebyu is in Tanintharyi. These are the clearest emerging hot spots and should be watched most closely.


New hot spot
Hkamti in northern Sagaing became a significant hot spot only in the final quarter. It had just 17 events in the whole period, so the result reflects its active neighbours more than the township itself. A new hot spot is an early signal. With so few events, it should be checked against local reports before it is used for planning.


Sporadic hot spots
Sporadic hot spots were significant hot spots in some quarters and never significant cold spots. This is the largest hot spot class, with 49 townships and 27.8% of all events. They include Kawkareik, Myawaddy and Hpapun in Kayin, Kale and Tamu in Sagaing, Hpakant, Myitkyina and Bhamo in Kachin, Muse in northern Shan, Maungdaw and Sittwe in Rakhine, and Hakha in Chin. Most are border or highland areas where fighting comes in waves. Their average count rose from 12 events a quarter in 2021 to a peak of 23 in 2023 Q4, and then settled at about 16. These places need flexible responses, because violence returns after quiet periods.


Oscillating hot spots
Oscillating hot spots are hot in the final quarter but were significant cold spots in at least one earlier quarter. There are 37 such townships, with 24.6% of all events. Ten are in Mandalay, nine in Sagaing and five in Magway, including Myaing, Madaya, Yesagyo, Pakokku, Sagaing and Myingyan. Three are in Rakhine (Kyaukpyu, Ann and Ramree) and three in Tanintharyi (Dawei, Palaw and Myeik). Their average count was below one event in 2021 Q1, so the cold quarters most likely come from the start of the period, when violence was concentrated in the cities. The average then rose to 26 events a quarter in 2023 and stayed near 20. Most of these townships are now long-running conflict areas rather than on-off areas.


No pattern detected
This class does not mean little violence. It includes Monywa (1,039 events) and Shwebo (806), two of the busiest townships, and it holds 25.5% of all events. A township falls here when its sequence of significant quarters does not match any EHSA rule. For example, a township that is hot in almost every quarter, but has a significant trend and a non-significant final quarter, fits no class. Fourteen of these townships are in Sagaing and eleven are in Rakhine. In Rakhine, a quiet 2023 followed by heavy fighting does not fit a single rule. These townships should be read together with the count maps, not ignored.


Oscillating cold spots
These eleven townships are cold in the final quarter but were significant hot spots at least once before. Five are in northern Shan, including Kutkai, Lashio and Laukkaing, five are in Yangon, and one is Paletwa in Chin. Their average count jumped to 33 events in 2023 Q4 and then fell to about 2 in 2025. In northern Shan, this matches a short and intense offensive followed by a sharp drop in reported fighting. In Yangon, the hot period was the urban violence of 2021.


Sporadic cold spots
This is the largest class overall, with 109 townships and 10.8% of all events. These townships were significant cold spots in some quarters and never significant hot spots. They include 28 Yangon townships, 14 in the Ayeyarwady delta, and townships in Magway, southern Shan and Bago (West). Some, such as Yedashe and Taungoo in Bago (East), have more than 190 events, but their neighbourhoods were quieter than the national average in some quarters. The average count was mostly between 2 and 5 events a quarter.


New, consecutive and intensifying cold spots
These classes describe places that became quieter. Chanmyathazi in Mandalay city is a new cold spot: its average fell from 27 events in 2021 Q4 to zero by mid-2025. Ten consecutive cold spots, nine of them in Yangon, such as Tamwe, Sanchaung and Ahlone, have been cold in every recent quarter. Their average fell from 4.6 events in 2021 Q2 to about one or less from 2023. Lanmadaw in Yangon is an intensifying cold spot. Together they show the end of the urban phase of the conflict in Yangon and Mandalay.


Persistent cold spots
Thirty-one townships were significant cold spots in at least 90% of the quarters with no significant trend. Ten are in Shan (East), six in Ayeyarwady, six in Shan (South) and five in Shan (North), including Tachileik, Kengtung and Mongla. Together they recorded only 198 events, and seven recorded none. These areas look stable in the data. However, part of eastern Shan is run by armed groups with long-standing ceasefires, and limited reporting may also make these areas look quieter than they are.



EHSA by event type
The three event types can follow different paths. I repeat EHSA for each type with the same settings.

Value added analysis: does the township boundary change the result?
Townships in Myanmar differ greatly in size. Some townships in Kachin and Shan are many times larger than townships in Yangon. A count in a large township is spread over a much larger area, and the result can change if the same events are grouped by other boundaries. This is the modifiable areal unit problem.
To test this, I repeat the Gi* and EHSA steps on a grid of equal area hexagons, using the same idea as the hexagons in Chapter 17. Each hexagon is 25 km across, about 540 sq km. Every event is counted in the hexagon that contains its point. If the main hot spots also appear on the hexagon grid, they are less likely to be an artefact of the township boundaries.

title: Take home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Integrated findings
The results from all methods fit together.

Violence is concentrated, and the concentration is stable at the core. The central dry zone, where Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay meet, is a High-High cluster, a Gi* hot spot and the largest group of hot spot classes. It holds 43% of the events and 52% of the reported fatalities. The hexagon analysis confirms it.
The fronts moved. Yangon and Mandalay cities were hot in 2021 and are now cold spots. Northern Shan flared in late 2023, Rakhine from 2024, and eastern Bago, Bago (West) and Kayin grew more slowly. The seven consecutive hot spots and the upward Mann-Kendall trends in Bago (West) point to where violence is building now.
The nature of violence changed. Air and drone strikes increased more than thirtyfold between 2021 and 2024, while IED attacks fell. Remote violence is the type with the widest hot spot area and with new and intensifying hot spots in previously quiet areas.
Most hot spots are unstable. Sporadic and oscillating classes cover 86 townships and more than half of all events. Only one township is a persistent hot spot.
The spatial unit matters. Township results are easy to link to administration and aid planning, but they overstate hot areas in large townships and hide urban clusters split across small townships. Using both units gives a fuller picture.

title: Take home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Implications for peace-building
This analysis can support peace-building and humanitarian work in a modest way. It shows where and when to look more closely. It does not explain why violence happens.

Protect civilians in the central dry zone. This is the core hot spot for every variable, including violence against civilians and fatalities. Humanitarian access, protection monitoring and support for displaced people should give it priority.
Use the emerging hot spots as early warnings. The consecutive hot spots, such as Nawnghkio, Kyaukme, Mogoke, Kyaukkyi, Shwegyin, Kyainseikgyi and Yebyu, and the upward trends in Bago (West) show where violence is building. Agencies can prepare supplies and contingency plans there before the situation peaks.
Plan for air and drone strikes. The rise in remote violence means that civilians can be harmed far from ground fighting. Community early warning, safe shelters and mine and explosive risk education matter even in areas without battles.
Stay flexible in sporadic and oscillating areas. Violence returns after quiet quarters. Re-running this EHSA every quarter with new ACLED data would turn the report into a simple monitoring tool.
Do not treat cold spots as safe. Cold spots may reflect limited reporting. Local partners should confirm the situation before resources are moved away from them.
Target within large townships. The hexagon results show which parts of a large township are active, which helps to place mobile clinics or distribution points.

The most important limitation is that ACLED records reported events. Media access, internet shutdowns and the presence of local monitors differ across Myanmar, so some quiet areas may simply be under-reported. Fatality numbers are estimates and are often conservative. The analysis also uses counts, not rates, so it shows where violence is concentrated, not the risk to an individual. Finally, the EHSA classes follow fixed rules. Small changes in the threshold, the time unit or the neighbour definition can move a township between neighbouring classes, so the broad families of hot spot, cold spot and no pattern are more reliable than any single class label.

title: Take home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Conclusion
Between January 2021 and September 2025, ACLED recorded 53,907 political violence events in Myanmar that could be placed in a township. The violence grew quickly after the coup, peaked in late 2023, and changed from bombings and attacks in towns to a wider war with more air strikes and shelling.
Global and local measures of spatial association show strong clustering. One main hot spot covers the central dry zone, and a smaller one follows the eastern borderlands. Emerging hot spot analysis adds the time dimension. Most hot spots come and go, the large cities have become cold spots, and a group of consecutive hot spots in northern Shan, eastern Bago, Kayin and Tanintharyi marks where violence is building now. The hexagon analysis confirms the main result but shows that the size of a hot spot depends on the spatial unit.
These findings can help humanitarian and peace-building actors decide where to look first and how often to update their view. They should be combined with local knowledge, population data and field reports before they are used for decisions.

title: Take home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
This report studies political violence in Myanmar from January 2021 to September 2025, using ACLED event data and the MIMU township boundaries. After cleaning, 53,907 events of three types remain: battles, explosions or remote violence, and violence against civilians. ACLED reports 89,012 fatalities for these events.
Violence rose quickly after the February 2021 coup, from 401 events in 2021 Q1 to 3,004 in 2021 Q4. It peaked at 4,026 events in 2023 Q4 and was still about 2,800 to 3,000 events a quarter in 2025. The type of violence also changed. Air and drone strikes rose from 88 events in 2021 to 2,977 in 2024.
The violence is strongly clustered. Global Moran’s I is between 0.45 and 0.56 for all five variables (p < 0.001). Local Moran’s I and Gi* agree on one main hot spot in the central dry zone, where Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay meet. These three regions hold 43% of the events and 52% of the reported fatalities. A smaller chain of hot spots runs along the Kayin and Tanintharyi borderlands. Cold spots cover eastern Shan, the Ayeyarwady delta and Yangon.
Emerging hot spot analysis shows that most hot spots are not stable. 37 townships are oscillating hot spots and 49 are sporadic hot spots, but only Pale is a persistent hot spot. Seven townships, in northern Shan, eastern Bago, Kayin, Tanintharyi and Mogoke, are consecutive hot spots. They became hot only in the latest quarters, and their average count rose from 9 events a quarter in 2021 to 43 in 2025.
A 25 km hexagon grid confirms the central hot spot, but only 52.6% of hexagons fall in the same broad class as their township. Large rural townships hide quiet areas, and Yangon’s many small townships hide an urban hot spot that faded after 2021.
The results show where reported violence concentrates and how it moves. They do not measure risk per person, because there is no population at risk in the data and reporting coverage varies across the country.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Question, data and approach


Question. Where did political violence concentrate in Myanmar, and how did these concentrations emerge, persist or fade between January 2021 and September 2025?
Data

ACLED event data: battles, explosions or remote violence, and violence against civilians.
MIMU Township Boundaries v9.4: 330 townships.
53,907 events kept after removing region-level locations and 3 events at sea; 89,012 reported fatalities.


Approach

Point-in-polygon join to townships and a township by quarter space-time cube (19 quarters).
Choropleth, point, yearly and state by quarter views.
Global Moran’s I, Local Moran’s I and Gi* with Queen neighbours (p < 0.05).
Gi* by quarter, Mann-Kendall test and emerging hot spot analysis (EHSA).
Value added: the same analysis on 25 km hexagons to test the effect of township boundaries.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Violence grew and changed form


Events rose from 401 in 2021 Q1 to 3,004 in 2021 Q4 and peaked at 4,026 in 2023 Q4. 2025 is still about 2,800 to 3,000 a quarter.
From 2023 Q4, remote violence exceeds battles. Air and drone strikes rose from 88 (2021) to 2,977 (2024), while IED attacks fell.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Where violence concentrates













Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay hold 43% of events and 52% of reported fatalities.
Busiest townships: Monywa (1,039), Kawkareik (946), Myaing (934), Kale (886) and Hpakant (854).
A second band of high counts follows the Kayin and Tanintharyi borderlands.
Eastern Shan and the Ayeyarwady delta report very few events.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
The fronts moved


Yangon was active in 2021 and quiet from 2023. Sagaing peaked above 1,000 events in 2022 Q3 and declined from 2024.
Northern Shan jumped to 878 events in 2023 Q4, Rakhine to 513 in 2024 Q1, and Bago grew steadily.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Clusters and hot spots













Strong global clustering: Moran’s I = 0.45 to 0.56, p < 0.001 for all five variables.
36 High-High townships and 34 Gi* hot spots, mostly in Sagaing, Mandalay and Magway.
A smaller hot chain in Kayin and Tanintharyi.
Cold spots: eastern Shan, the delta and Yangon. Cold does not mean safe, since reporting may be thin.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: Hot spots by type of violence
text:
Hot spots by type of violence


All three types share the central dry zone hot spot. Battles add Tanintharyi and the Kayin border; remote violence adds eastern Bago.
Violence against civilians is concentrated almost only in the central dry zone and Tanintharyi.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Emerging hot spots






















Only Pale is a persistent hot spot. 49 sporadic and 37 oscillating hot spots hold 52% of events.
7 consecutive hot spots (Nawnghkio, Kyaukme, Mogoke, Kyaukkyi, Shwegyin, Kyainseikgyi, Yebyu) are building now.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
How the EHSA classes changed


Consecutive hot spots rose from 9 to 43 events per township and quarter (2021 to 2025). Oscillating cold spots in northern Shan and Yangon peaked in 2023 Q4 and then fell sharply.
“No pattern detected” still includes Monywa and Shwebo, two of the busiest townships.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Does the spatial unit matter?













The central dry zone hot spot appears at both scales.
Only 52.6% of hexagons share their township’s class. Within township hot spots, many hexagons are cold, because events follow roads and towns.
Yangon is cold at township level but a fading hot spot on hexagons, because its 45 small townships split the events.
Use townships for administration and hexagons for targeting.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Findings, limits and implications


Findings

One stable core: the central dry zone, with 43% of events and 52% of fatalities.
Cities cooled after 2021. New fronts opened in northern Shan, Rakhine, Bago and Kayin.
Most hot spots come and go. Seven consecutive hot spots are building now.


Limitations

ACLED counts reported events. Access and coverage vary.
Counts, not rates: there is no population at risk.
EHSA labels depend on the rules, the time unit and the neighbours.


Implications for peace-building

Prioritise civilian protection and access in the central dry zone.
Use consecutive hot spots and rising trends as early warning.
Prepare for air and drone strikes beyond front lines.
Re-run EHSA every quarter and confirm cold spots with local partners.
